title: Are AI Agents The New Semiconductor IP?
gist: AI agents are emerging as a reusable, rapidly customizable design capability akin to semiconductor IP, pushing EDA toward consumption/token-based pricing, MCP-modularized tools and platform disaggregation. Executives from ChipAgents, Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens EDA, Keysight, Arm, Silvaco, Cognichip and Movellus flag multi-agent orchestration, siloed data and the $500M cost of a leading-edge mistake as key brakes on autonomy.

insights.claim: ChipAgents says it can customize AI design agents for a specific customer flow in as little as the same day, versus roughly 10 months for a traditional customized soft-IP engagement.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Agent vendors compress the customization cycle that soft-IP licensors monetize; watch for pricing pressure on custom IP services.
insights.quote: With IP, you need 10 months. Our cycle is much shorter because AI agents are very easy to customize. In some cases we can give solutions to the customer the same day.
insights.locator: “We have in-house specialized AI agents

insights.claim: ChipAgents runs in-house specialized AI agents covering spec analysis, RTL generation, formal and functional verification, CDC linting and place-and-route, sold both as optimized agents and as customer-specific builds resembling the IP licensing model.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Startups are attacking the full front-to-back EDA flow with agents, not single point tools — a competitive vector against Synopsys and Cadence.
insights.locator: “We have in-house specialized AI agents

insights.claim: Unlike narrow, costly soft-IP customization that often fails to transfer to derivative chips and multi-die assemblies, AI agents can customize functions with little human intervention, self-optimize for workloads, and even adjust for aging hardware — though experienced engineers must still verify results.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Agentic design capability could become a new reusable, licensable asset class alongside traditional IP blocks.
insights.locator: At the leading edge, soft IP developers

insights.claim: Agentic AI is not expected to replace traditional semiconductor IP but to change the design process in which that IP is used, including automating porting, optimization and validation of soft IP across process nodes.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Near-term risk to IP vendors is margin on services/porting, not displacement of core IP licensing.
insights.locator: While agentic AI won’t replace traditional IP

insights.claim: Cadence argues that agents drive much heavier EDA tool usage because they run many experiments to find answers quickly, making consumption-based licensing a natural next step after the industry's earlier move from perpetual to time-based licenses.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Agent-driven usage growth under consumption pricing could lift EDA revenue intensity per customer; watch Cadence/Synopsys licensing disclosures.
insights.quote: They’re hitting up the tool usage even more because they want to find answers quickly, and they’re trying lots of experiments.
insights.locator: “If you look at how the EDA industry has evolved

insights.claim: According to Silvaco CEO Wally Rhines, no EDA vendor appears to price by tokens yet, but customers are all discussing it, and Silvaco is open to selling agents (e.g. for manufacturing-equipment calibration) billed on token consumption so proprietary customer data is never exposed.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Token-based EDA pricing is a live but unrealized business-model shift; first mover could reset industry pricing.
insights.quote: It doesn’t seem like anyone is, but their customers are all talking about it.
insights.locator: “There are some things where you’d really rather sell an agent

insights.claim: Synopsys describes moving from teams of engineers coordinated by a human manager to a hierarchy of agents spanning EDA implementation and sign-off plus CAE solvers (CFD, HFSS electromagnetics, mechanical), mirroring PPA trade-offs like clock gating that cut power but increase area.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Synopsys is positioning its combined EDA+simulation portfolio as the substrate for multi-agent design orchestration.
insights.quote: But what was happening by a team of engineers coordinated by a human manager is now being done by a hierarchy of agents with that framework.
insights.locator: That creates a new hierarchy in the design flow.

insights.claim: Synopsys frames the evolution of AI in EDA as three stages: tool acceleration for better PPA (DSO.ai), GenAI script/assistant tools (e.g. Fusion Compiler setting questions), and now hierarchical multi-agent frameworks mimicking engineering org structures.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Useful map to judge where each EDA vendor's AI roadmap sits.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, the adoption of agents continues to grow.

insights.claim: Arm reports hyperscalers are now asking what agentic AI needs from the CPU, because coordinating many parallel agents demands CPU-level orchestration, bandwidth and memory, unlike batched training jobs where the CPU mattered less.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Agentic workloads strengthen the case for higher CPU content per AI rack (Arm Neoverse/CSS, x86) — a CPU:GPU ratio shift.
insights.quote: The transition that we see when we talk to hyperscalers is now about what they need from the CPU.
insights.locator: “What’s different about traditional AI and agentic AI

insights.claim: Movellus CEO Mo Faisal says the industry has swung from 'everything is going to be a GPU' to CPUs and GPUs at a one-to-one ratio, comparing it to the early-2000s shift to multicore and an architectural churn that recurs every 10 to 15 years.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Supports rising CPU attach rates in AI infrastructure.
insights.locator: “I draw parallels to the early 2000s gigahertz wars

insights.claim: Arm is considering modeling agentic workloads in pre-silicon to shape future IP, CPU design and its CSS offerings for customers building their own chips.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Signals Arm roadmap tuning toward agent-orchestration CPUs.
insights.locator: “There could be a time where we start looking at agentic workloads

insights.claim: Cognichip warns that multi-agent orchestration will be an increasingly big challenge: models lack deep chip-physics understanding, agents may disagree and cause ping-pong convergence issues, and in heterogeneous multi-die stacks the combination yields 'chaos times chaos.'
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Expect slower, more cautious adoption of autonomous agents in advanced-packaging design flows.
insights.quote: You put them all together and you get chaos times chaos.
insights.locator: “Orchestration is going to be a big challenge

insights.claim: ChipAgents says very large SoCs require multi-agent systems with parallel access to different contexts for debugging and formal verification, and predicts future 'virtual chip companies' staffed by virtual AI engineers.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Long-run bull case for agent vendors: lower barriers to forming chip design houses.
insights.quote: In the future, we’re going to have virtual chip companies with virtual AI engineers working together
insights.locator: Establishing a hierarchy for agents is important

insights.claim: Keysight expects agentic workflows to disaggregate sticky EDA platforms, and is taking an open approach — playing to its simulation strengths and offering orchestration help — while the most sophisticated customers build their own workflows.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Disaggregation threatens platform lock-in that underpins Cadence/Synopsys moats; open-tool vendors may gain share.
insights.quote: One of the key implications of agentic workflows is disaggregation
insights.locator: “One of the key implications of agentic workflows

insights.claim: EDA vendors must modularize products behind MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers with Python APIs and documentation/examples so customer agents can stitch together code-based workflows; Keysight says front-runner customers are already building such agentic workflows.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: MCP readiness becomes a competitive checkbox for EDA and simulation vendors.
insights.quote: That means we need MCP servers, and we need all the proper documentation so we can train these agents.
insights.locator: That requires some fundamental changes for EDA companies.

insights.claim: Cadence argues EDA is uniquely suited to agentic AI because decades-old tools can objectively grade agent decisions (e.g. whether a floor plan lowered power), so no human is needed to judge each result, and it is applying agents plus physics-based simulation to data center design tooling.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Built-in verification loops make EDA one of the more credible domains for agent monetization.
insights.quote: EDA has the tools that we’ve used for decades to grade the decisions.
insights.locator: “When you look at how we’re applying agents

insights.claim: Siemens EDA cites a $500 million cost of a mistake at 3nm or 2nm, arguing engines must remain deterministic and high-fidelity regardless of the AI techniques used.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Extreme cost of failure caps how much autonomy agents get in sign-off, favoring incumbents with trusted engines.
insights.quote: The cost of a mistake is $500 million at 3 or 2 nanometers
insights.locator: “The cost of a mistake is $500 million

insights.claim: Training chip-design AI is constrained because design data is siloed, customers demand on-prem deployment, and foundries tightly restrict PDK access — agents handle language well but physics remains the big challenge.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Proprietary data access (foundry/EDA partnerships) is the moat for chip-design AI; pure-play AI startups face data scarcity.
insights.quote: But the physics component is still the big challenge.
insights.locator: “All of these agent technologies and models

insights.claim: Cognichip notes that because billions of hardware examples are unavailable and siloed, the industry is shifting intelligence from the model into the agent, making systems 'top-heavy' and prone to losing balance.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Architectural fragility of chip-design agents is an underappreciated execution risk.
insights.quote: that makes it top-heavy, and top-heavy things tend to lose their balance.
insights.locator: “The model brings a lot of intelligence

insights.claim: Movellus says agents should manage the hardware running agents (racks, thermals, workload orchestration), but the silicon industry is among the slowest and most conservative adopters given $500 million program-failure risk.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Expect demand for infrastructure-management agents, but slow uptake inside chip design itself.
insights.quote: A $500 million silicon program failure is a big deal.
insights.locator: “Should agents be managing the hardware
